newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia coffee exporters urged to target gourmets.
newsitem.headline: Colombia coffee exporters urged to target gourmets.

text.p: Colombian coffee exporters were urged to focus more closely on the specialty coffee market in the United States Friday -- a market still growing by about 10 percent a year despite the overall decline in U.S. coffee consumption.
The advice came in an address by Emilie Kendall, head of beverage marketing for Dunkin' Donuts, to an annual meeting in this Caribbean port city of Colombia's National Coffee Exporters' Association.

"You can leverage your established brand awareness into many, many channels," Kendall told the meeting, noting that Colombian coffee and its "Juan Valdez" trademark carried enormous weight among U.S. consumers.

"Consumers are drinking less coffee, but they're drinking better coffee," Kendall said, explaining how specialty coffee remained a growth industry in the United States despite flat or negative growth in overall coffee consumption.
"It's a force that's changing the coffee industry in the United States dramatically," Kendall added of the trend toward flavored coffees, gourmet blends and cozy coffee cafes.

She did not elaborate on how Colombia could take better advantage of the trend. But John Naranjo, commercial manager of the powerful National Coffee Growers Federation, told the exporters' meeting earlier Friday that roasters have complained in the past about Colombia being overly aggressive in seeking to deal directly with the so-called "end users" of Colombian coffee.
"The explanation for this is that producer countries are considered possible or potential competitors in the end sale of the product," Naranjo said.
"Furthermore," he added, "it would seem that the interest of roasters is concentrated increasingly in boosting their own participation in the market, rather than in making the market grow."

Dunkin Donuts, which Kendall said sells more than 600 million cups of coffee a year, is the biggest U.S. coffee retailer. It earned about $650 million from coffee sales last year alone, rivaling the $680 million it made from its world famous donuts.

Kendall said the chain offers a blend of Colombian, Brazilian and Central American beans. Defying the trend toward specialty brews, she said surveys showed most Dunkin loyalists took no interest in the bean count, however.
"They're much more concerned with the end product than with what went into it," she said.
